title: A second mutation routed through MutationObserver vs done inline
variable: observer-driven follow-up mutation vs a direct one
claim: Antipattern #40 from web-performance-antipatterns-50.md: 'MutationObserver / event handlers that themselves mutate, cascading invalidation waves.' Observers are how loosely-coupled UI reacts to state it does not own, and the cost is invisible at the call site - the code that writes an attribute has no idea a callback will run and write three more.
result: CONFIRMED, modestly: Script 1.25x / 1.39x / 1.58x, growing with element count, with a Coherent_JSEvent phase present only in B. Styles is flat throughout, which is the point - both variants perform exactly the same two attribute writes per tile, so the ratio is the observer machinery itself rather than any extra invalidation. Routing a reaction through MutationObserver costs roughly 25-60% more JS-thread time than calling the same code directly. That is a real but affordable price for the decoupling it buys, and it is much smaller than the costs this batch found in innerHTML += or full list rebuilds. Remember the scope: this measures a cascade one hop deep, not the runaway self-observing form the antipattern warns about, which does not converge and cannot be measured.
notes: Applicability gate: ADAPTED. MutationObserver is flagged missing in the feature inventory but exists and works - verified against the Player: observe() was accepted, callbacks fired, records were delivered with correct targets, and a mutation performed inside the callback applied. THE ADAPTATION, and why: the antipattern's pure form is a callback that mutates what it observes, which does not converge - it is an unbounded feedback loop and would measure a hang rather than a cost. This case therefore makes the cascade exactly one hop deep: the observer watches #watched and writes to #mirror, which it does not watch. That keeps it terminating and, more importantly, keeps the two variants doing IDENTICAL work - the same two attribute writes per tile per frame - so the ratio isolates the observer machinery itself rather than counting extra mutations. Read it as 'what does routing a reaction through MutationObserver cost', not as 'what does a runaway cascade cost'. Rule 1: one variable, whether the second mutation goes through the observer. Rule 2: identical DOM - both variants build the same tiles and markers in the same places. Rule 3: identical JS apart from the single USE_OBSERVER constant; both pages construct the observer and tag the tiles, so only observe() and the inline write differ. Rule 4: no text, no assets. Rule 5: at 300, tiles and markers share the 92x68 grid and occupy 1852x1032 inside 1920x1080, with markers sitting directly below their tile. Rule 6: the mutation loop IS the case, but it CANNOT replace the shared damage driver here - the attribute writes change nothing visible, so the first draft of this case rendered nothing at all and the smoke pass caught it reporting an absent GPU phase. Both variants therefore also run the shared root-nudge driver, identical in each, so the engine genuinely re-renders every frame and the observer comparison sits on top of a live page rather than an idle one. Rule 7: attribute values derive from the frame counter. Rule 8: counts 30/100/300. Rule 9: plain HTML/CSS/JS. Rule 10: expected axis is Script - observer bookkeeping and callback dispatch are JS-thread work. TIMING NOTE: observer callbacks are asynchronous, so B's second mutation lands slightly later in the frame than A's. Both still complete within the frame, and the end state is identical.
